title: About the CRISC exam
description: What the CRISC exam looks like, how to read and answer its questions as a risk practitioner, how to pace and prepare, how to book it, and how passing turns into certification. Written in plain language by KaiSip from ISACA's published information.
disclaimer: KaiSip is an independent study app. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by ISACA. CRISC® is a registered trademark of ISACA, used here only to describe the exam. ISACA alone sets the exam rules and decides eligibility and certification. No study app can promise a pass, including this one.
check_before_booking: Fees, rules and requirements on this page were checked on the date shown. They can change, so check isaca.org before you book.

sections.title: The exam at a glance
sections.summary: A 4-hour, computer-based exam of 150 multiple-choice questions, scored on a scale from 200 to 800. A score of 450 or higher passes.
items: 150 multiple-choice questions in 4 hours (240 minutes). Each question has four options and one best answer, and may be written as a question or as an incomplete statement.
Some questions share a short scenario, so you read the situation once and answer two or more questions about it.
Scores are scaled from 200 (the lowest) to 800 (every scored question answered correctly). You pass with 450 or more.
Scaling keeps different versions of the exam comparable and fair, so 450 is not a fixed percentage of questions.
Some questions are unscored pretest items, and you cannot tell which. Treat every question as if it counts.
There is no penalty for a wrong answer: your score is based only on the questions you answer correctly. Answer every one.
Your results show how you did in each domain. That breakdown is for your information only and does not change your score.
Languages: English, Spanish and Japanese, as listed in ISACA's current candidate guide. Choose your language when you register.
You take it on a computer, either at a PSI test center or online with a remote proctor.
The current content outline took effect in 2025, and the updated exam has been offered since November 3, 2025.
ISACA describes CRISC as covering emerging technology, including assessing AI risk and AI data governance and ethics. Expect AI questions in any domain.

sources.label: ISACA press release: CDPSE and CRISC exam updates (2025)

sections.title: The four domains and their weights
sections.summary: ISACA's content outline splits the exam into four domains. A domain's weight is its share of the exam, so it is a good guide to where your study time goes.
items: Domain 3, Risk Response and Reporting, is the largest at 32%, nearly one question in three. Give it the most practice time.
Domains 1 and 3 together make up 58% of the exam. Governance ideas such as ownership, appetite and lines of defense show up in every domain.
Domain 4 is the smallest at 20%, yet still about one question in five. Its technology topics are tested through a risk lens, not as technical how-to.
Behind the outline, ISACA lists 24 supporting tasks, such as building risk scenarios, defining key risk indicators (KRIs) and running tabletop exercises. Most questions put you in one of those tasks.
Read every question as the risk practitioner unless it tells you otherwise: you identify, analyze, recommend and report, while the business owns the risk.

sources.label: ISACA Exam Candidate Guide (2026), Appendix B: CRISC outline

sections.title: How CRISC questions are built
sections.summary: Questions test whether you can apply risk concepts and standards at work, not recall definitions. Most offer several sensible actions, and only one is the best answer to what is asked.
items: ISACA writes each question to measure practical knowledge and the application of general concepts and standards, with one best answer among four options.

Many questions are short workplace situations: an organization, a named role, something that has changed, and what to do, who decides or what matters most. Others are one-line questions with no scenario.
Expect the wrong options to be reasonable actions. They usually lose because they come too early, belong to someone else, fix a symptom or ignore appetite, not because they are false.
A priority word such as FIRST, BEST or MOST LIKELY decides which of several true options wins. ISACA's own exam tips tell you to watch for these qualifiers.

A useful habit: rule out the options topic knowledge eliminates, such as one that mixes up appetite and tolerance or a KRI and a key performance indicator (KPI), then choose among the rest with judgment.
Other roles appear in questions: the IS auditor, the CISO, IT, internal audit and the board. Their jobs are real, but unless the question asks about them, answer as the risk practitioner.
AI and machine-learning risk is treated like any other risk: it needs a business owner, an assessment against appetite and monitoring once it is in use.

sources.label: ISACA Exam Candidate Guide, version 1.26 (2026), section 3.1: Exam Questions and Exam Tips

sections.title: Read each question as a risk practitioner
sections.summary: A short routine for every question: find what is asked, who you are and where the risk sits in its cycle, then eliminate and choose.
steps: Read the last line first. Note what is asked for: an action, a person, a document, a metric or a cause.
Find the priority word, such as FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST or MOST LIKELY, and hold it in mind while you read the options.

Check the role. You are the risk practitioner: you analyze, advise, facilitate, monitor and report. Risk owners decide, control owners answer for their controls working, and the board and senior management set appetite and tolerance.
Place the risk in its cycle: identified, analyzed, compared with appetite, treated, validated, reported. The best answer is usually the next step that has not happened yet.
Rule out the options topic knowledge eliminates, often two. Compare what is left: which comes first, which the others depend on, who should act, and which serves business objectives.
Say in one sentence why your choice beats the runner-up. Then answer and move on.
items: The business owns risk. The practitioner never accepts a risk or approves an exception, and an option where they pick the treatment alone is usually a trap.
Business objectives first: a risk matters by its effect on what the enterprise is trying to achieve, not by its technical score.

Appetite and tolerance drive the response. Within appetite, the owner can accept and monitor; above it, the owner treats the risk with your advice, and only the level that set the limit can approve carrying it.

Analyze before acting: a new threat, finding or change is assessed and its owner told before controls are chosen, unless the question says that is already done. In a declared incident, containment comes first.
Not the auditor and not the security manager: giving audit opinions and running the security program are other people's jobs in a CRISC question.

sections.title: Priority words and what they ask
sections.summary: Many questions carry a priority word, such as BEST or MOST LIKELY, as ISACA's exam tips note. When several options are true, it decides which wins. The readings below are KaiSip's habits.
items: FIRST: a question of sequence. Look for the step everything else depends on, often understanding objectives, finding the owner or assessing the risk, before any treatment.
BEST: the most complete and fitting answer for the situation and your role. It usually addresses the cause, respects appetite and leaves the decision with the owner.
MOST, as in MOST important, effective or appropriate: rank the options on the exact quality named. MOST effective favors the control that works on the cause; MOST appropriate favors the right role.
PRIMARY: the main purpose, reason or concern, not a side benefit. Ask what the thing exists to do, such as a KRI warning before the loss.
GREATEST: the biggest effect, usually on business objectives or overall exposure. Weigh business impact and likelihood together, not technical severity alone.
MOST LIKELY: probability, not severity. Pick the explanation or event that best fits all the facts given, even if another would be worse.
LEAST: negative questions using NOT, EXCEPT or LEAST are rare on CRISC-style items. If a practice question uses one, the test is inverted: find the option that helps or fits least.

sections.title: Common traps by domain
sections.summary: Each domain has a few traps that catch prepared candidates. Most swap the risk practitioner's job for someone else's, or act before the risk is understood. These are KaiSip's patterns, organized by ISACA's domains.
items: Governance: naming IT, the CISO, a vendor or a committee as the risk owner. The owner is one business manager accountable for the objective at stake.
Governance: the practitioner setting appetite or tolerance, or approving the framework. The board and senior management decide; the practitioner supplies analysis and options.
Governance: treating a clean compliance result as proof of low risk. Compliance is a minimum, and risks no rule covers still need assessment.
Risk Assessment: copying a severity score or a business impact analysis (BIA) ranking in as the risk rating. Risk needs likelihood and business impact, on one shared scale.
Risk Assessment: counting approved or untested controls in today's rating. Current risk counts only controls in place and shown to work; planned ones give future residual (target) risk.
Risk Response and Reporting: recommending the strongest control. The best response brings risk within appetite at a cost no greater than the loss it avoids.
Risk Response and Reporting: choosing a lagging KRI, such as last year's incidents, or reporting a fix as done on the owner's word. Prefer leading indicators and evidence.
Risk Response and Reporting: holding a confirmed tolerance breach for the next report. Escalate it promptly to the risk owner and the level that set the limit.
Technology and Security: banning or adopting a new technology or AI tool before assessing it. Record it with a proposed business owner and assess it against appetite first.
Technology and Security: choosing faster restores for repeat incidents, or more general training for a problem in one role. Look for the root cause.

sections.title: Pacing your 4 hours
sections.summary: 240 minutes for 150 questions is 96 seconds each. Aim for about 90 seconds a question so you keep some time in hand at the end.
items: Checkpoints at about 90 seconds a question: reach question 40 by the 1-hour mark, question 80 by 2 hours and question 120 by 3 hours. That leaves about 15 minutes in hand.
If a question stalls you, choose your best answer and move on. A blank earns nothing, and a wrong answer costs nothing extra.
Breaks: up to two, each 10 minutes or less, with the proctor's permission. The exam clock keeps running, so a break uses your time.
Scenario questions take longer and short ones take less. Judge your pace at the checkpoints, not on any single question.
A tutorial on using the exam screens runs before the exam starts. Follow it closely so you know how to move around before your time begins.

sections.title: Your last week before the exam
sections.summary: A calm seven-day plan: one full timed practice early, then shorter recall work led by domain weight, and rest at the end.
steps: Seven days out: sit one full timed practice exam of 150 questions in 4 hours. Then sort each miss by cause: a content gap, or a thinking slip such as the wrong role.
Six days out: about 90 minutes on the two heaviest domains, Risk Response and Reporting first, then Governance. List the key rules from memory, then check them against your notes.

Five days out: Risk Assessment. Recall inherent, current, residual and future residual (target) risk, likelihood and impact, the BIA and the risk register, then do a short untimed set and read every explanation.
Four days out: one short timed practice set across all four domains. Review every miss and name the principle each one tested.
Three days out: Technology and Security through a risk lens, plus the principles you slip on most. No timed tests from today on.
Two days out: light review. Recite the priority words and the reading routine from memory, then check. Confirm your ID, appointment time and travel or online setup.
One day out: rest. Look over your own short list of rules, get ready for the morning, and sleep at your usual time.
items: Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with the next one. Never double up.
Recall beats rereading: answer from memory first, then check. Spaced practice and a good night's sleep help more than a late cram.
Practice scores in any study app, including KaiSip, are not ISACA scaled scores and cannot predict your result.

sections.title: Registering and fees
sections.summary: You register and pay through your ISACA account, then book a date with PSI. You have 6 months from registering to sit the exam.
steps: Create an ISACA account. Use your name exactly as it appears on the government-issued ID you will bring on exam day.
Check that a PSI test center near you has dates, or run PSI's compatibility check on the computer you will use online. A company computer may need your IT team's approval.
Register for the exam and pay in full. Registration is open all year, and your 6-month eligibility period starts on the day you register.
From 48 hours after you pay, book your date with PSI through your ISACA account. Dates open up to 90 days ahead.
items: Exam fee: US$575 for ISACA members, US$760 for non-members. Your price depends on whether you are a member when you register.
Fees are not refunded and cannot be transferred. If your 6 months end before you sit the exam, the fee is lost.

Need more time? You can buy one 6-month extension for US$75. It appears on your dashboard from 30 days before to 30 days after your eligibility ends. Cancel any booked date at least 48 hours ahead first.
Reschedule free of charge up to 48 hours before your appointment. Within 48 hours, you either sit the exam or lose the fee.
Missing your appointment, or arriving more than 15 minutes late, also loses the fee.

For a genuine hardship, such as sudden illness, a death in your immediate family or a traffic accident, contact PSI within 72 hours of the missed appointment, with documents. If PSI declines, you register and pay again.
Special testing accommodations are requested when you register, once the fee is paid, and must reach ISACA at least 4 weeks before your preferred date.

sections.title: Test center or online
sections.summary: You can sit the exam at a PSI test center or online with a remote proctor. Follow ISACA's guide and your check-in specialist, and ask ISACA support if unsure.
items: Test center: arrive at least 30 minutes early and plan where your belongings will go; a locker or set area holds them. You may share the room with other test takers, and some noise is normal.
Online: test your computer with PSI's compatibility check before you register. A work computer may block the exam software or need your IT team's approval.

Before an online exam you scan the room: all four walls, your desk including under the keyboard, and from floor to ceiling. You can use an external webcam, a mirror with your laptop camera, or your phone.
A mirror check follows, showing the screen, keyboard and every edge of your laptop or monitor. If you use a phone for either step, move it out of the testing area afterward.
Online rules: no one else in the room, no talking or reading aloud, no food, drink or gum, and keep facing the screen. Breaking a rule can void the exam without a refund.
Chat with the remote proctor is in English only.

sections.title: Exam day
sections.summary: Bring one valid ID, arrive or log in early, and leave everything else behind.
items: Bring one current, original, government-issued ID showing your name, photo and signature. Copies, handwritten IDs and digital IDs are not accepted.
Your first and last name must match your registration. Without acceptable ID you cannot sit the exam, and you lose the fee.
Nothing comes in with you: no notes or paper, calculator, phone, smartwatch, smart glasses, headphones or bag, and no food or drink, not even water.
You may take up to two breaks of 10 minutes or less, with the proctor's permission. The exam pauses, but the clock keeps running.
Screenshots and photos of any part of the exam, including the results screen, are not allowed.
Pace: 240 minutes for 150 questions is 96 seconds a question. Answer every one; a blank earns nothing.

sections.title: After the exam
sections.summary: A preliminary pass or fail shows on screen when you finish. The official result follows within 10 working days.
items: Your official score arrives by email and in your MyISACA account within 10 working days.
Results show your scaled score and how you did by domain. They do not show which questions you got wrong.
If you did not pass, you can ask for a rescore in writing through ISACA support within 30 days of your results. The fee is US$75.
Retakes: up to four attempts in the 12 months from your first. Wait 30 days before the second attempt, then 90 days before each later one. Each attempt costs the full fee.
If you pass, you cannot sit the CRISC exam again during your 5-year window to apply.
Passing is not the same as being certified. You still need to apply, as the next section explains.

sections.title: Becoming and staying certified
sections.summary: After passing, you apply with proof of work experience, then keep the certification current with yearly learning and a fee. ISACA decides every application.
steps: Wait for your official score, then apply within 5 years of passing. You may sit the exam before you have the experience.
Show at least 3 years of work experience in IT risk management and information systems (IS) control, across at least two of the four CRISC domains, gained in the 10 years before you apply.
Have your supervisor or manager verify your experience.
Agree to ISACA's Code of Professional Ethics and its continuing professional education (CPE) policy, and pay the US$50 application fee.
items: CRISC allows no experience waivers or substitutions, unlike CISA.
ISACA's pages word the experience requirement slightly differently, so read the current application form before you apply.
Keeping CRISC: earn at least 20 CPE hours a year and at least 120 over each 3-year period, related to CRISC work.
Annual maintenance fee: US$45 for members, US$85 for non-members, due by January 1.
ISACA audits a random sample of CPE records each year. If you are selected and cannot support what you reported, you lose the certification.
